content: Palliative care standards must be developed with the active involvement of a wide range of stakeholders. This ensures that the services provided meet the minimum requirements necessary to deliver effective care. The primary goal of these standards is to enhance the quality of care for all patients with life-threatening illnesses, including vulnerable populations such as children and individuals with low incomes. These standards should be grounded in the latest evidence-based practices in palliative care and should define core functions that are optimal, achievable, and measurable. Regular monitoring of the implementation of these standards is essential to ensure their effectiveness. The development of palliative care standards serves several critical purposes. They provide a shared understanding of the work to be done and establish a benchmark for the quality of service delivery. They help maintain the quality of care as service coverage expands and facilitate continuous improvement by identifying areas requiring corrective action. Additionally, these standards inform patients and their families about the level of care they can expect and demand, guide staff on their responsibilities, and serve as a resource for training in palliative care. The creation and implementation of a palliative care plan must be periodically monitored and evaluated to ensure that its objectives are being met. This evaluation process requires careful design and planning, beginning early in the programming phase. A basic information system should be established at the outset to collect the necessary data for ongoing monitoring and evaluation. The performance of palliative care activities can be assessed using a quality improvement framework, and guidance is available for evaluating cancer control programs, including palliative care, through frameworks such as those provided by the World Health Organization (WHO). An evaluation plan must clearly define who will evaluate the implementation of palliative care activities, what aspects will be evaluated, the core indicators and their respective standards, the design and methodology to ensure credibility, and how the results will be used to improve performance. Examples of structure, process, and outcome indicators, along with their associated standards, can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of palliative care programs. Palliative care is a vital component of comprehensive cancer control programs. It addresses the needs of patients with advanced cancer and their families, linking with cancer prevention, early detection, and treatment strategies to address all priority needs within a community. This integration ensures the efficient use of limited resources. A cancer palliative care program should also be part of a broader strategy that addresses the needs of patients with other chronic life-threatening conditions, such as HIV/AIDS, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and chronic respiratory diseases. Evidence-based standards for palliative care services are essential to improve clinical and organizational practices across all settings. Simple, low-cost public health models of palliative care can be implemented to reach the majority of the target population, particularly in low-resource settings where most cases are diagnosed at advanced stages. These models emphasize the integration of palliative care services into existing health systems at all levels, with a particular focus on communityand home-based care. The WHO emphasizes that palliative care should evolve in response to national needs and experiences. Countries are encouraged to share their successes and request information relevant to their specific needs. The availability of opioids for cancer pain management, the assessment of system barriers, and the implementation of WHO guidelines are critical components of effective palliative care. Additionally, complementary and alternative therapies, as well as public health approaches to palliative care, are important considerations in addressing the needs of patients and caregivers. In conclusion, palliative care is a key element of cancer control strategies, addressing the needs of patients and families while making efficient use of resources. It is essential to develop evidence-based standards and integrate palliative care into existing health systems to ensure access to quality care for all patients, particularly in low-resource settings.
